title: Poisson mean under H0 for a longer interval
source: Theory S2-2.5 Quick check 1 (mean 0.8 per week over 5 weeks gives lambda=4); new integer products
stem: Under the null hypothesis the number of events per week has mean {k|int}. A test uses a period of {n|int} weeks. What is the value of \(\lambda\) under \(H_0\) for the total number of events in that period?

steps.name: A
steps.note: A is n k. Original n=5, k=4 gives 20. (The teaching example 0.8 x 5 = 4 is a different illustration in the page, not this original.)

title: Null-hypothesis mean over several months
source: Theory S2-2.5 Quick check 2 (monthly mean 3 over 4 months gives lambda=12); new positive integers
stem: Under \(H_0\) the monthly mean is {m|int}. A test is based on a period of {t|int} months. What is the value of \(\lambda\) under \(H_0\)?

steps.name: A
steps.note: A is m t. Original m=3, t=4 gives 12.

title: The integer significance level as a percentage
source: Theory S2-2.5 Quick check 3 (a 5% test uses significance level 5); new conventional levels 1, 2, 5, 10
stem: A hypothesis test is to be carried out at the {s|int}% significance level. What number, as a percentage, is the significance level?

steps.name: A
steps.note: A equals s. Original s=5 gives 5. The constraint (s-1)*(s-2)*(s-5)*(s-10)==0 restricts s to the usual textbook levels 1, 2, 5 and 10.

title: Poisson test of a reduced mean number of sports injuries

source.note: Stem taken from the QP PDF (UCLES 2017), Question 6 parts (i), (ii) and (iii) only, including the opening context. Official answers and mark allocation from the MS PDF. The item is paper/self-mark. Part (iv) is a normal approximation for a 36-month period and is omitted (that skill is section S2-2.4).

stem:
This question is 9709/71/M/J/17 Question 6(i), (ii) and (iii), taken from the official QP.

The number of sports injuries per month at a certain college has a Poisson distribution. In the past the mean has been 1.1 injuries per month. The principal recently introduced new safety guidelines and she decides to test, at the 2% significance level, whether the mean number of sports injuries has been reduced. She notes the number of sports injuries during a 6-month period.

(i) Find the critical region for the test and state the probability of a Type I error.  [6]

(ii) State what is meant by a Type I error in this context.  [1]

(iii) During the 6-month period there are a total of 2 sports injuries. Carry out the test.  [3]

steps.name: L
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): B1 for 6.6 (could also be scored in (iii)).

steps.name: P1
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): M1, allow an incorrect lambda in both probabilities. Independent: exp(-6.6)*7.6=0.010336... which is 0.0103 to 3 s.f.

steps.name: P2
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): M1 for the P(X<=2) expression. Independent: exp(-6.6)*29.38=0.039973... which is 0.0400 to 3 s.f. (or 4 d.p.).

steps.name: Both
steps.text_tex: Both probabilities are 0.0103 and 0.0400, to the accuracy required.
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): A1 for both values.

steps.name: CR
steps.text_tex: Since \(0.0103\lt 0.02\) and \(0.0400\gt 0.02\), the critical region is \(X\leqslant 1\).
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): DA1 for CR is X<=1, dependent on at least one M. The mark field records A1; the official D (dependent) prefix is noted here.

steps.name: TI
steps.text_tex: The probability of a Type I error is \(\mathrm{P}(X\leqslant 1)=0.0103\).
steps.note: Official MS 6(i): B1FT, follow through their P(X<=1).

steps.name: CTX
steps.text_tex: A Type I error would be wrongly concluding that the mean number of sports injuries has decreased.
steps.note: Official MS 6(ii): B1, must be in context.

steps.name: H
steps.note: Official MS 6(iii): B1, can be scored in (i). Allow mu or lambda / 1.1 or 6.6.

steps.name: IN
steps.text_tex: The observed total 2 is not in the critical region (equivalently, \(\mathrm{P}(X\leqslant 2)=0.0400\gt 0.02\)).
steps.note: Official MS 6(iii): M1 for 2 not in the critical region, or for comparing P(X<=2)=0.0400 with 0.02.

steps.name: CON
steps.text_tex: There is no evidence that the mean number of injuries has decreased.
